question.prompt:
Each of the five numbers \(1,\) \(4,\) \(7,\) \(10,\) and \(13\) is placed in one of the five squares so that the sum of the three numbers in the horizontal row equals the sum of the three numbers in the vertical column. The largest possible value for the horizontal or vertical sum is

[Figure 1](figures/1999_AMC_8_Q11_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
The number \(1\) must belong to the horizontal row, the vertical column, or both. The other two numbers on any line containing \(1\) add to at most \(10+13\), since these are the two largest available numbers. Thus that line has sum at most
\[
1+10+13=24.
\]
Because the horizontal and vertical sums are equal, neither can exceed \(24\).

We can attain this bound. Put \(13\) in the center, \(1\) and \(10\) in the left and right squares, and \(4\) and \(7\) in the top and bottom squares. This uses each number exactly once and gives
\[
1+13+10=4+13+7=24.
\]
Therefore the largest possible sum is \(\boxed{24}\), choice \(\text{D}\).
solutions.title: Use the line containing 1

solutions.explanation:
Adding the horizontal and vertical sums counts every outer number once and the center number twice. This makes the center the only number whose position affects the combined total.

Let \(c\) be the center number and \(S\) the common sum. Since the five numbers total \(35\), we have
\[
2S=35+c.
\]
The center cannot exceed \(13\), so
\[
2S\leq35+13=48,
\qquad S\leq24.
\]
To reach \(24\), put \(13\) in the center. The remaining numbers can be paired as \(1+10=11\) and \(4+7=11\). Put one pair in the two horizontal outer squares and the other pair in the two vertical outer squares. Both sums are then \(13+11=24\).

Thus the largest possible sum is \(\boxed{24}\), choice \(\text{D}\).
solutions.title: Add the two equal sums
Check each center and its pairings
